title: Claude AI for marketing: How teams use it with HubSpot
content:
I’ve been experimenting with Claude AI for marketing workflows over the past year, and it’s now my go-to assistant. In this field, AI use is close to universal: 98% of marketing teams use it in some way, according to HubSpot’s State of AI in Marketing report . For campaign marketers, that might look like turning a product announcement into a week of social posts, tightening ad copy to fit character limits, or pressure-testing campaign messaging before a stakeholder review.
But Claude only knows what you tell it. It can’t automatically see which contacts converted, which campaigns generated pipeline, or what customers keep asking your support team, so even sharp output can miss what’s actually happening in your business.
The HubSpot connector for Claude brings your HubSpot CRM data into the conversation and lets Claude act on it, like drafting a marketing email or creating a follow-up task directly in your account. This guide covers how to set up the connector, the marketing workflows and prompts it supports, how to govern its use, and when a dashboard is the better choice.
Claude AI for marketing means using Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, to handle the writing, research, and analysis work that campaigns depend on. Claude helps marketers draft, analyze, and summarize work, such as writing and editing first drafts, turning meeting notes into briefs, and assembling campaign readouts from numbers in separate analytics tools. It can also pull current information from the web, which makes it handy for early-stage market research.
As with all large language models (LLMs), the quality of Claude’s output depends heavily on the context it receives. Anthropic’s prompting guidance compares Claude to a sharp new employee with no background on how your team operates, and it recommends telling Claude who the output is for and how it will be used.
Claude works well on its own for one-off drafting and research. It becomes far more powerful once it can read your real customer records, campaign results, and engagement history.
Picture a marketer asking Claude why last quarter’s webinar series underperformed. Without a link to HubSpot, Claude can only work with what gets pasted into the chat: an exported spreadsheet, a few copied metrics, a paragraph describing the audience. Each fresh analysis means exporting and explaining that background again, and the answer stops wherever the export does.
Connected workflows move that context gathering out of the marketer’s hands. The HubSpot connector for Claude links HubSpot context to Claude, giving it read access to contacts, deals, campaigns, marketing emails, and other records, scoped to each person’s current HubSpot access rights. Logged calls, meetings, emails, tasks, and notes are readable too, unless the account has Sensitive Data turned on. The webinar question can now pull event records, follow-up activity, and campaign attribution data into a single answer.
The connection also runs in reverse. Claude can create and update HubSpot records, such as changing a deal stage or adding a task, from the chat window, though it can’t delete data.
HubSpot Smart CRM unifies customer context and campaign records. It sits beneath Marketing Hub, Sales Hub, and HubSpot’s other core products as their shared database, showing where each contact stands at every point in the relationship. Claude then works from one consistent record rather than fragments stitched together from separate tools. Connected AI workflows improve personalization and execution for that reason.
Getting there takes a one-time setup in Claude’s connector settings.
The HubSpot connector for Claude is free, but it requires a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) and an active HubSpot user account on any plan, including free. Super Admins and users with App Marketplace Access permissions can connect immediately; everyone else needs Super Admin approval first.
Toggling HubSpot on under + > Connectors in any chat lets Claude reference your HubSpot records in its answers. Set the connector’s Write tools option to Needs Approval , as HubSpot recommends, so Claude confirms each proposed edit with you before making it. Every create or update action is recorded in HubSpot’s Audit Log and attributed to both the user and the connector, and bulk edits run in batches of 10 records or fewer.
HubSpot’s marketing examples include ranking last month’s campaigns by revenue, finding the subject lines that drew the most clicks, measuring how long contacts stayed in each lifecycle stage, and queuing follow-up tasks for recent email openers. Claude can also publish a blog post once the prompt supplies a title, author, featured image, meta description, and slug. Workflows are the exception: Claude drafts the content, and you build the workflow in HubSpot, where marketing automation runs.
With the HubSpot connector in place, Claude supports four everyday marketing jobs: analyzing campaigns, drafting content and email, tailoring outreach, and even serving as a virtual assistant for routine marketing tasks. It follows the access rules already set in HubSpot, so results depend on what the signed-in user is allowed to view and change.
Campaign records, attribution data, and marketing email performance are all readable, so one prompt can compare a campaign’s engagement with its attributed results. Prompts about individual page or post performance must name a campaign and a date range, and drafts return only metadata. Results can come back as charts, such as a pie chart isolating contacts who opened an email but never clicked. For AI analytics use cases beyond the connector, see AI marketing analytics .
HubSpot Content Hub supports content creation and publishing workflows. Through the connector, Claude can create and update landing pages, website pages, and marketing emails, and page designs built in Claude Design can be sent into HubSpot. Campaigns are writable too: Claude can create one and attach new assets, so a launch email and its landing page start out grouped together. Ask Claude to study your recent top-performing emails before it drafts the next one.
Claude can read segments (lists) but can’t create them, so building segments stays in HubSpot. Use Claude instead to trace a contact’s conversations across chat, email, and SMS before tailoring outreach. Inbox and help desk conversations add another source of buyer language: Claude can summarize the month’s most common questions, surfacing recurring concerns in customers’ own words. For events, Claude can take an imported registrant list and produce follow-up emails. From there, Claude can match registrants to existing contacts and update lifecycle stages, subject to any conditional property rules configured in HubSpot.
After a sales call or campaign debrief, a single plain-language request can log the notes, create follow-up tasks, and update a contact’s lead status. Our guide on using Claude as a virtual assistant shows a comparable follow-up routine that stays inside Claude: Project instructions define how to track action items, and uploaded meeting transcripts supply the notes.
Recurring report prep suits Claude marketing automation in Claude Cowork: A skill stores your prep steps, and a scheduled task runs them remotely, even while your computer sleeps. Tasks that need local files or apps run only on your machine. Claude can then turn that prep into a team doc or a one-slide leadership summary.
Each prompt below opens by assigning Claude a role. Anthropic’s prompting guide lists role-setting among its core techniques and says even a one-line role steers what Claude focuses on and how it sounds. The rest names the records to pull, the work to produce, any HubSpot action, and the answer format. Swap in your own bracketed details, then save the versions that work as a team library of Claude prompts for marketers.
Pro tip: Once a prompt proves useful week after week, turn it into one of your team’s Claude skills . A skill stores the parts of a prompt that never change, like the role, the HubSpot records to check, and the output format. Claude recognizes when a request calls for that skill and applies it without being asked, so teammates only need to supply details like the campaign name and date range.
“You’re a marketing analyst reporting to a CMO. Pull the HubSpot campaign record and marketing email results for [Campaign Name] from [date range]. Compare open rates with click rates, break down engaged contacts by lifecycle stage, and show the campaign’s attributed revenue. Return a three-bullet summary, then a comparison table. Cite the HubSpot records behind each figure.”
This prompt grounds a Claude AI marketing strategy in deals you’ve already won:
“You’re a campaign strategist for a [industry] company. Review our closed-won deals from last quarter and identify the buying triggers that appear most often. Use them to draft a four-week launch plan for [Product] with audience criteria from our existing segments, a three-email nurture outline, and a landing page structure. Then create a campaign in HubSpot called [Campaign Name].”
The connector can’t edit a campaign once it exists, so confirm the name and details before you approve Claude’s proposal.
“You’re a content marketer. Read last month’s inbox and help desk conversations in HubSpot. List the five most common questions or objections, each with a short example of how customers phrased it. Then suggest 10 blog headlines and five email subject lines that answer them in the same vocabulary.”
“You’re an email copywriter focused on re-engagement. Find contacts who opened [Email Name] but didn’t click, and group them by lifecycle stage. For the largest group, draft one follow-up email that offers a 15-minute demo. For any customer example, use only these details: [case study summary]. Create it in HubSpot as a marketing email so I can review it before it goes out.”
“You’re a GTM strategist preparing a sales handoff. Pull the full engagement history for [Company Name] in HubSpot, including emails, meetings, calls, and notes. Summarize it in three short paragraphs: background and key stakeholders, open challenges and recent interactions, and recommended next marketing touchpoints.”
HubSpot acknowledges that Claude’s answers can be wrong and advises having a person check them. Adding “cite the HubSpot records behind each figure” to any analysis prompt lets you open each record and confirm the number. Before running a write prompt across many records, test it on one, and read each proposed change before typing Yes. Drafted emails and pages still need a brand voice and a link check in HubSpot before they are published.
Turning those individual checks into a repeatable team process is the job of governance.
Governing Claude AI for marketing comes down to four controls: skill review, shared standards, connector access, and measurement. Together, these controls also build the readiness that HubSpot’s guide to AI agents for marketing links to success with agentic AI: clear processes and steady testing.
Dashboards support recurring KPI monitoring better than ad hoc AI analysis. Questions that repeat on a fixed cadence, like weekly lead volume against goal or monthly pipeline created, deserve a saved report that answers them without anyone typing a prompt.
HubSpot dashboards group related reports on one screen for a specific audience or goal. Owners control access by keeping a dashboard private, opening it to the whole account, or limiting it to chosen users and teams. Report emails can run on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule, and dashboard emails can recur as well, though only HubSpot users can receive the recurring versions. Each recipient gets the same report configuration every cycle, with no prompt involved.
Claude covers the questions nobody has built a report for. Saved reports and dashboards don’t appear among the objects the HubSpot connector for Claude can read, so Claude works from records such as contacts, deals, campaigns, and marketing emails instead. That suits one-off, multi-condition questions, like which contacts opened a launch email in the past two weeks, have an open deal, and haven’t heard from sales since. Claude also handles the conversation and help desk summaries mentioned earlier, where the answer is a pattern in written text.
The Claude Cowork scheduling from the follow-up section still fits here: It can draft commentary on recurring numbers while the numbers themselves stay on a dashboard.
Teams get the most from running the two in sequence:
The HubSpot connector for Claude installs without code. You need a paid Claude subscription plus an active HubSpot user account at any edition, even free. Open Claude’s Settings > Connectors , click Browse , find HubSpot, click Connect , and sign in to grant permissions. Unless you’re a Super Admin or have App Marketplace Access, a Super Admin approves it first.
Strong prompts give Claude a job title, the HubSpot records to check, and an output shape. For email, have Claude write a follow-up for contacts who opened a send without clicking, saved as a HubSpot marketing email. Ads differ: Since the connector can’t create them, Claude drafts headline variants from help desk objections for your ad platform.
For brand voice, convert your style guide into a skill that Team and Enterprise owners can provision org-wide. For compliance, set Write tools to Needs Approval so every edit waits for your Yes.
Rely on dashboards for metrics your team revisits every week or month, since HubSpot can email those reports automatically. Turn to Claude for unplanned questions that combine several filters and for themes hidden in support conversations. Dashboards aren’t on the connector’s readable object list, so Claude pulls numbers straight from deals, campaigns, and other records.
Measure time and money separately. Clock a repeat task, like a campaign recap, now and again once Claude handles it. Team and Enterprise owners can see connector users, read and write action counts, and estimated time saved in Claude’s analytics. For money, Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise include a campaign ROI report weighing revenue against spend.
